tapeLine: The Fed delivered the near-lock: the FOMC voted 12-0 Wednesday to raise rates a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, its first hike since July 2023, and Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters “the plain fact is inflation is too high” while declining to commit to a path — “I'm not in the forward guidance business,” per CNBC's Wednesday meeting coverage. The dot plot itself did commit, penciling in one more 2026 hike toward roughly 4.00%-4.25%. Stocks, which had traded higher into the decision, sold off during Warsh's press conference: the Dow fell 631.21 points (−1.21%) to 51,461.90, the S&P 500 fell 0.45% to 7,551.81, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.01% to 25,978.42, while the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 5% to 5.016%. Futures point to a Thursday recovery — Dow +0.7%, S&P 500 +0.8%, Nasdaq-100 +1.1% — helped by oil easing as Saudi Arabia moves to restore half its damaged East-West pipeline's capacity within days, with full repair now put at roughly six weeks. Initial jobless claims, housing starts and the Philly Fed survey are due at 8:30 ET, the first data since the blackout lifted.
matters:
The Fed did what was priced: the FOMC voted 12-0 Wednesday to raise the federal funds rate a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, the first hike since July 2023, confirming the roughly 92% odds this brief has tracked since Tuesday. Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters “the plain fact is inflation is too high” and that most global economies face similar price pressure, while pointedly declining to pre-commit to what comes next: “I'm not in the forward guidance business,” per CNBC's Wednesday meeting coverage. The Summary of Economic Projections did the guiding instead — the median dot now shows one further hike in 2026, toward a 4.00%-4.25% range, with inflation projections marked up into the mid-to-high 3% area for the year.

Markets read the press conference as more hawkish than the vote itself. All three major indexes had traded higher earlier Wednesday but turned lower as Warsh spoke: the Dow fell 631.21 points (−1.21%) to 51,461.90, the S&P 500 fell 0.45% to 7,551.81, and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.01% to 25,978.42. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 5% to 5.016%, matching the multi-decade highs set earlier in the week, per CNBC's bond-market coverage. Thursday futures point to a partial recovery — Dow +0.7%, S&P 500 +0.8%, Nasdaq-100 +1.1% — per Bloomberg's live markets coverage.

The oil-pipeline story moved from dispute toward a resolution that splits the two competing claims this brief has tracked since Monday. Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Saudi Arabia is seeking to restore only about half the East-West pipeline's capacity within days, with full capability now targeted in roughly six weeks — landing at the upper end of Reuters' three-to-six-week sourcing, not U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright's flatter “measured in days” framing. Oil eased Thursday morning on the news: Brent traded near $105.81 and WTI near $102.14, both down slightly, per CNBC's Thursday oil coverage.

The AI-slowdown story continued to run on a separate, political track from monetary policy. Dario Amodei's proposal to deliberately slow frontier AI development, and Beijing's dismissal of it as “fearmongering,” remain unresolved ahead of U.S.-China AI discussions expected before the Trump-Xi summit on September 24 — a date now on the calendar that gives this thread a concrete resolution point it lacked earlier in the week.

On the financing thread this brief has tracked since 10 September: no new debt-financed sponsor buyout has printed since Sequence Holdings/DFO's mostly-equity purchase of Baldwin Group on 14 September. That test is still open three days later, now running alongside a higher-rate environment that makes fresh leveraged deals structurally harder to price.

Invalidation: the dot plot's single additional 2026 hike is itself a call on data that hasn't happened yet; a soft initial-claims or housing print Thursday, or a much larger one, would move the odds priced for that second hike more than anything said Wednesday.

regime.tag: Post-hike: dot plot flags one more 2026 hike, pipeline resolving in stages, financing test still open
regime.sizing: Wednesday's hike and Warsh's press conference resolved the near-term Fed question but opened a new one: the dot plot's single additional 2026 hike is itself unconfirmed by data. The pipeline dispute is resolving toward Reuters' longer estimate rather than the Energy Secretary's shorter one, in stages rather than all at once. The financing test set on 10 September remains open with no new candidate, now running against a higher policy rate than when the test began.

secondOrder: Four threads carried through the Fed decision rather than resolving with it. The Fed thread resolved on the vote but reopened on the dot plot: Wednesday's 25bp hike was the near-lock outcome this brief has tracked since Tuesday, but the median projection for a second 2026 hike is a fresh, unpriced call that Thursday's jobless-claims and housing data will start to test. The oil thread took its first real step toward resolution: Saudi Arabia's own timeline — half capacity in days, full capacity in about six weeks — is closer to Reuters' three-to-six-week sourcing than to Wright's flatter days-only framing, which this brief flagged as the optimistic outlier on Monday. The AI thread stayed exactly where it was, still political rather than monetary, but picked up a concrete date: the Trump-Xi summit on 24 September gives the Amodei-Beijing dispute a deadline it did not have earlier in the week. And the financing thread stayed open for a fourth straight session, with no new debt-financed buyout since Baldwin on 14 September — a silence that now has to be read against a policy rate that just moved higher, not just against the absence of a deal.

scorecard.text: The 16 September brief put Wednesday's hike odds at roughly 92%, a near-lock. That landed exactly: the FOMC voted 12-0 to raise rates a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, its first hike since July 2023, per CNBC's Wednesday meeting coverage.

This brief has sided with Reuters' three-to-six-week pipeline estimate over U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright's “measured in days” framing since Monday. Wednesday's Bloomberg reporting resolved the split in that direction: Saudi Arabia is targeting only about half of pipeline capacity restored within days, with full repair put at roughly six weeks — the upper end of Reuters' range, not Wright's.

The financing test set on 10 September — a large, freshly debt-financed sponsor buyout printing — is still open. No new candidate has emerged since Sequence Holdings/DFO's mostly-equity purchase of Baldwin Group on 14 September, and the test now runs against Wednesday's higher policy rate rather than into it.

The 15 and 16 September briefs treated the Amodei/China AI-slowdown story as detached from Fed policy. That held through the rate decision itself — zero linkage between the two stories in Wednesday's coverage — and the thread now has a concrete date, the 24 September Trump-Xi summit, rather than drifting indefinitely.
